items.prompt: Which statement best defines constructive feedback?

options.label: Praise given regularly to keep the person motivated, whatever the results turn out to be
A general opinion about how good someone is at their job, shared once a year at review
Specific information about behaviour and its impact, given to help the person improve
A complete list of every mistake the person has made since they joined, shared at once

rubric: Constructive feedback is specific, behaviour-focused and aimed at improvement.
Distractors describe vague judgement, fault-listing or praise only.

items.prompt: In the SBI feedback model, what do the letters stand for?

options.label: Standard, Blame, Instruction
Strength, Barrier, Improvement
Summary, Benefit, Intention
Situation, Behaviour, Impact

rubric: SBI means Situation, Behaviour, Impact.
Other options are plausible-sounding but invented.

items.prompt: Which feedback is specific?

options.label: "You never listen to your colleagues, and it shows in every meeting we have."
"Your attitude lately has been a problem for the team, so please fix it soon."
"In today's 10am meeting you interrupted Sam three times while she presented."
"You come across as quite disrespectful in meetings, and people have noticed it."

rubric: Specific feedback names an observable behaviour, time and context.
Distractors are vague labels or sweeping generalisations.

items.prompt: Which term describes feedback that focuses on what a person did rather than on who they are?

options.label: Global feedback
Behavioural feedback
Character feedback
Personality feedback

rubric: Behavioural feedback targets observable actions.
Other terms refer to judging the person.

items.prompt: What is the usual recommended timing for giving feedback on a specific event?

options.label: After several weeks, so emotions have cooled fully
Only at the annual review, so it is all together
Only after the person asks for it directly
Soon after the event, while details are fresh

rubric: Timely feedback is more accurate and useful.
Delaying until reviews or waiting for requests loses relevance.

items.prompt: Which of these are recommended habits when receiving feedback? Select all that apply.

options.label: Immediately explain why the giver is wrong
Listen without interrupting
Ask for a specific example you did not understand
Only accept feedback that comes from your own manager

items.prompt: Priya is preparing to give a team member feedback about missed deadlines. Her manager reminds her to start from a recommended first step in preparation. Which step should Priya take first?

options.label: Decide on consequences if it happens again
Gather specific examples of the missed deadlines
Ask colleagues what they think of his work habits
Write up the personality flaws behind his lateness

rubric: Preparation begins with concrete, factual examples.
Distractors skip evidence or shift to personality and gossip.

items.prompt: Why is "You are lazy" poor feedback?

options.label: It names the person, but feedback should avoid addressing anyone directly
It judges the person and names no behaviour, so invites defensiveness
It is too harsh in tone, though the label itself is accurate and useful
It is too short to be clear, since longer comments are usually better

rubric: Labels attack identity and give nothing to change.
Length is not the issue; feedback is still addressed to the person.

items.prompt: Why does describing the impact of a behaviour help in feedback?

options.label: It makes the feedback sound formal, so it is taken seriously
It shows why the behaviour matters, which motivates change
It replaces describing the behaviour itself, keeping feedback brief
It proves the person was wrong, so they accept blame

rubric: Impact links behaviour to consequences, giving a reason to change.
Impact complements, not replaces, the behaviour description.

items.prompt: Which comment is an example of positive reinforcing feedback?

options.label: "That was fine, nothing to mention really, so keep going as you have been."
"Good effort overall, though everything could still be better next time."
"Your clear agenda kept the meeting to 30 minutes, so we finished early."
"Great job today, you're wonderful to have around and everyone appreciates you."

rubric: Reinforcing feedback names the behaviour and its benefit.
Distractors are vague praise or mixed messages.

items.prompt: What does the "feedback sandwich" (praise, criticism, praise) risk doing?

options.label: Burying the main message so the person misses the change
Making the person feel the criticism was a minor, optional point
Making criticism clearer because the praise gives it context
Making the person trust later praise more because it came first

rubric: The sandwich can dilute the key message and make praise seem insincere.
Other options claim benefits it does not reliably give.

items.prompt: A colleague says, "Your report had several errors." Which response shows good receiving of feedback?

options.label: "Everyone makes errors; yours get ignored too."
"Can you show me which parts had errors so I can fix them?"
"Okay." followed by saying nothing more and changing nothing.
"I was rushed because of the team's late data."

rubric: Asking for examples shows openness and seeks clarity.
Other responses deflect, excuse or disengage.

items.prompt: Which of these explain why feedback should focus on behaviour rather than personality? Select all that apply.

options.label: Behaviour can be observed and agreed on, so both people start from the same facts
Behaviour can be changed more easily than a trait, so the person has a clear next step
Personality comments are more honest, so they show the person where the real problem lies
Behaviour feedback is safer because it avoids the need for any specific examples

items.prompt: Omar tells a junior colleague, "Your presentation was a mess." The colleague looks upset and asks what he means. Omar wants to rephrase it as good feedback. Which rewording best fits?

options.label: "Other people on the team present better than you and don't make these mistakes."
"Your slides had 200 words each, so the audience read instead of listening."
"I expected much more from you than that presentation, given how well you prepared."
"Your presentation skills are generally weak right now, and they need to improve soon."

rubric: It names observable behaviour and its effect.
Distractors remain vague, personal or comparative.

items.prompt: Which statement is the most specific piece of feedback?

options.label: You need to be more professional with all of our clients, especially the key accounts.
You never seem to listen to what our customers are telling you on the phone.
Your attitude in meetings has become a problem for the whole team lately.
In Tuesday's call you interrupted the client twice before she finished.

rubric: It names an observable action, with time and example, that the person can recognise.
The distractors use vague labels or generalisations that give nothing concrete to act on.

items.prompt: Why is feedback usually framed around observable behaviour rather than personality traits?

options.label: Behaviour can be pointed to and changed, whereas labels invite defence.
Personality is never relevant to how well someone performs at work.
Describing behaviour lets the giver skip explaining the impact it had.
Labels are fine but they simply take longer to explain than actions.

rubric: Behaviour is concrete and changeable, so people can respond without feeling attacked.
Distractors wrongly claim traits are irrelevant or that impact need not be explained.

items.prompt: A manager says, "You always miss deadlines." What is the main weakness of this comment?

options.label: It mentions deadlines, which are not an appropriate topic for feedback.
It is too gentle, so the person will not realise how serious the issue is.
It generalises with 'always' and cites no example, so it feels like an attack.
It looks to the future rather than the past, which confuses the listener.

rubric: Sweeping words like 'always' with no example trigger defensiveness and give nothing to act on.
Other options misjudge the tone or claim deadlines are off-limits.

items.prompt: Why is it generally best to give feedback soon after the event?

options.label: Quick feedback removes any need for a later follow-up conversation.
Details are fresh, so the person can recall the event and act on it.
Emotions are at their peak, so the person will be more receptive to hearing it.
Waiting lets the giver collect more incidents before they speak up.

rubric: Timeliness keeps the example clear and relevant for the person receiving it.
Distractors treat strong emotion or stockpiling incidents as benefits, which they are not.

items.prompt: When receiving feedback, what is the main purpose of asking a clarifying question?

options.label: To check you understood what was meant before you decide how to respond.
To show the giver how their feedback could have been better worded.
To challenge the giver's example until they agree to withdraw it.
To buy time so that the conversation ends sooner than planned.

rubric: Clarifying ensures you respond to what was actually meant.
Distractors turn questions into a defensive or evasive tactic.

items.prompt: Which of these are features of constructive feedback? Select all that apply.

options.label: It suggests a change or next step the person could try.
It is saved up and delivered at the annual review.
It describes a specific example that was observed.
It explains the effect the behaviour had on the work or team.
It sums the person up with a label such as 'careless'.

rubric: Constructive feedback is specific, explains impact and points to a way forward.
Saving it up and using labels reduce clarity and trust.

items.prompt: Priya's manager reads her report and says, "Good job on the report," then moves on. Priya wants to keep improving her reports. Why is this comment of limited use as feedback?

options.label: It should have included some criticism so the comment felt balanced.
Positive comments cannot guide improvement, only criticism can do that.
It was too brief to be polite, which will slowly damage her trust.
It does not say what was good, so Priya cannot repeat it deliberately.

rubric: Without a specific example, Priya does not know which behaviour to repeat.
Distractors wrongly say praise cannot help or that criticism is needed for balance.

items.prompt: Sam talked over colleagues in Monday's meeting, and Lena then stopped sharing ideas. Which statement applies the situation-behaviour-impact approach correctly?

options.label: Sam, Monday's meeting felt tense, and I think your attitude toward colleagues was the reason for it.
Sam, in meetings lately you have not been a team player, and that is hurting the whole group.
Sam, you are a dominating person, and I have noticed the team dislikes working with you.
Sam, in Monday's meeting you talked over Lena twice, and she stopped sharing ideas.

rubric: It states the situation, the observed behaviour and its impact.
Others use labels, vague advice or leave out who did what.

items.prompt: While you give feedback, an employee says, "That's not fair!" and crosses their arms. What is the best next step?

options.label: Acknowledge how they feel, restate the example calmly, then ask their view.
Drop the issue for now and revisit it later, so the working relationship stays comfortable.
End the talk and send the feedback in writing instead, so it avoids a conflict in person.
Repeat the point more firmly and stress the consequences, so they understand how serious it is.

rubric: Acknowledging emotion and inviting their view keeps the example on the table without escalating.
Distractors escalate, avoid or abandon the feedback.

items.prompt: A team member sent a client email with a pricing error. You need to give corrective feedback. What is the best way to deliver it?

options.label: Talk to them privately that day or the next, once you have both calmed down.
Save it for the quarterly review with their other development points.
Raise it at the next group meeting as a general reminder to everyone.
Post it in the team chat that afternoon so everyone can learn from it.

rubric: Private and prompt delivery protects dignity and keeps the example fresh.
Public or delayed options embarrass the person or dilute the message.

items.prompt: A colleague tells you your slides were too dense for the client. Which response best applies good practice for receiving feedback?

options.label: Point out two things they could improve in their own slides.
Say nothing for now and decide later whether it applies to you.
Thank them, ask which slides felt dense, and say what you will change.
Explain that the client asked for detail, so the slides were fine as they stood.

rubric: Thanking, asking for specifics and committing to action shows openness.
Distractors justify, avoid or deflect.

items.prompt: A team member calmly handled an angry customer. Which comment is the most effective way to praise them?

options.label: Thanks for handling that, I know customers can be difficult at times.
Great work today, you are a real star performer on this team.
You let her finish, then offered a fix, and she stayed with us.
Well done, keep on doing whatever it was you did with that customer.

rubric: It names specific behaviours and the result, so the person can repeat them.
Others are generic and don't say what was done well.

items.prompt: You are preparing for a corrective feedback conversation with a team member. Which steps should you take? Select all that apply.

options.label: Decide what change you hope the conversation will lead to.
Note one or two specific, recent examples.
Think about how they may react and how you will respond.
Plan to raise every concern from the past year.
Prepare a label that sums up their character.

rubric: Good preparation includes concrete examples, a clear aim and anticipating reactions.
Listing every past concern and using labels overload and provoke defensiveness.

items.prompt: You told Omar that his handover notes missed key details, and he agreed with the examples. The conversation is nearly over. Which closing step best fits good practice?

options.label: Thank him and trust that he will sort it out on his own.
Tell him you will now monitor all of his work more closely.
Agree one concrete change and a date to check in together.
Ask him to write an apology to the colleagues affected.

rubric: A specific agreed action with a follow-up turns feedback into change.
Distractors leave it vague, damage trust through surveillance, or add punishment.

items.prompt: Priya interrupted three colleagues in Tuesday's meeting, and the team stopped sharing ideas afterwards. Which statement best applies the situation-behavior-impact model?

options.label: "You are a dominant person in meetings, and it leaves the team feeling unheard and discouraged."
"In Tuesday's meeting you interrupted three people, and the team went quiet for the rest of it."
"In meetings you often come across as rude, so please try to be more respectful to everyone."
"On Tuesday several people seemed annoyed with you, so I think you need to listen better."

rubric: The key names the situation, an observable behavior and its concrete impact.
Distractors use trait labels or vague impressions, which are judgments rather than observations.

items.prompt: Dev made an error on a client call at 10am, and his manager is still angry at midday. Which action best applies good timing and setting principles for feedback?

options.label: Wait until calm, then hold a private conversation that day or next morning, citing specifics
Join the call's follow-up in front of the client to correct the error on the spot
Save it for the annual review so it can be discussed alongside the rest of his performance
Raise it at the next team meeting so everyone learns from the error while it is fresh

rubric: Feedback should be timely, private and given when the giver is calm.
Public correction and long delays both reduce trust and learning.

items.prompt: Your manager tells you, "Your client emails are unclear." You want to act on it. Which response best applies good practice for receiving feedback?

options.label: Ask for a recent example and what clearer looks like, then summarise what you heard
Ask which clients complained and what they said, so you can judge how serious the criticism really is
Explain that your workload leaves little time to polish emails, so the quality is understandable
Agree immediately and promise to rewrite every email more carefully from now on

rubric: Asking for a concrete example and clarifying turns vague feedback into something actionable.
Explaining, over-promising or hunting for sources avoids the content of the feedback.

items.prompt: You must give feedback to a team member about repeatedly missed deadlines. What is the best first step in preparing?

options.label: Draft a script of compliments to open with so that the person stays relaxed throughout
Collect specific dated examples and decide what change you want to see afterwards
Decide the consequences you will apply if the person does not accept the feedback
Ask teammates whether they agree the person is unreliable before you raise anything

rubric: Preparation starts with factual examples and a clear desired outcome.
Distractors rely on scripts, gossip or threats instead of evidence.

items.prompt: A manager wants to turn "You need to be more proactive" into feedback the employee can act on. Which rewrite is best?

options.label: "Please show more initiative on projects and take ownership of more tasks in the team."
"Next sprint, please flag any blocker at standup on the day you hit it, not at the deadline."
"I'd like you to anticipate problems earlier and communicate more with the people involved."
"Try to be proactive in the way you approach upcoming sprint work and the team's goals."

rubric: The key states a specific, observable action with a time frame.
The distractors restate vague traits in different words.

items.prompt: You have just described a specific behavior to a team member. Which next moves fit good feedback practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: Explain why you believe they did it deliberately
Describe the effect it had on the team's work
Add earlier unrelated mistakes to show it is a pattern
Ask for their view of what happened
Agree a specific next step and a follow-up date

rubric: Good practice invites dialogue, makes the impact clear and closes with an agreed action.
Piling on past errors or guessing at motives triggers defensiveness.

items.prompt: You tell Sam that his shift handovers lack detail. He crosses his arms and says, "Nobody else gets criticised for this." You have two dated examples of thin handovers from this month. What is the best next move?

options.label: End the conversation and send a written warning so the issue is formally recorded
Acknowledge his reaction, restate the specific handover example, and ask for his view
List other colleagues' handover faults to show that you are treating everyone fairly
Tell him the issue is minor and move on, since pushing now would only create a bigger argument

rubric: Acknowledging emotion and returning to the specific example keeps the conversation on facts.
Comparing others, escalating or minimising each avoid the issue or damage trust.

items.prompt: A manager told an analyst, "You're careless." Over the next month the analyst's errors continued unchanged. Which is the most likely cause of the feedback failing?

options.label: It came too soon after the errors, so the analyst had no chance to fix them on their own
It was given in private, which made the analyst feel the issue was less important to the team
It labelled a trait without naming any observable behavior, so nothing concrete could be changed
It contained too much positive framing, so the analyst did not take the message seriously

rubric: Trait labels give the recipient no specific behavior to change.
The distractors blame factors, such as privacy or softness, that the stem does not support.

items.prompt: A manager always gives praise, then criticism, then praise. Team members now brush off her compliments and say, "Here comes the but." What best explains this?

options.label: Praise has become a predictable cue for criticism, so it loses credibility and blurs the message
The criticism is too short, so the team cannot tell how serious the problem actually is
The team lacks emotional intelligence and cannot separate positive comments from negative ones
People dislike receiving praise and so ignore it whenever it is offered by a manager

rubric: A fixed formula makes praise a warning signal and dilutes both praise and critique.
Other options misattribute the pattern to dislike of praise or to the team's skills.

items.prompt: Two managers give the same factual feedback about late reports. Manager A's employee improves; Manager B's does not. A asked for the employee's view and agreed actions together; B just told the employee what to do. Which difference best explains the outcomes?

options.label: B's employee was probably less capable, so the same feedback was less likely to produce any result
A's approach created shared ownership of the fix, while B's left only an instruction
B gave the feedback too soon after the lateness, before the employee had time to reflect on it
A's feedback was more detailed, which made the problem seem larger and more urgent to the employee

rubric: Two-way dialogue and agreed actions build commitment, unlike one-way instruction.
The stem says the content was the same, so detail or ability explanations do not fit.

items.prompt: A manager says: "Your presentation was disorganised, and honestly everyone thought so. Fix it by Friday." Which flaw most undermines this feedback?

options.label: It addresses a single presentation, so it is too narrow to show the employee any pattern in their work
It sets a deadline before the employee has been asked for their view, which pressures them before they understand
It is stated directly, and blunt feedback triggers defensiveness more than a gently hinted suggestion would
It cites unnamed others and gives no observed example, so the employee cannot verify or act on it

rubric: Appeals to unnamed consensus and the lack of an example make the claim unverifiable.
A deadline and directness are not the core flaw; specificity and evidence are.

items.prompt: A peer you dislike tells you harshly, "You dropped the ball on the handover." You think the tone is unfair, but you did skip a handover step last week. What is the best analysis?

options.label: Separate the delivery from the content, then check the claim against what happened
Accept it all as true, since a harsh peer is probably being honest about everything
Dismiss it entirely, since feedback delivered with a hostile tone cannot be reliable
Raise the peer's tone first and refuse to discuss the handover until it improves

rubric: Evaluating content separately from delivery lets you use valid feedback from a poor messenger.
Rejecting or accepting everything wholesale ignores the evidence.

items.prompt: A feedback conversation escalated into an argument within minutes. Which features of how it was set up likely contributed? Select all that apply.

options.label: It was based on a secondhand report that was never verified
The manager cited specific dates and examples
The manager asked for the employee's view before drawing conclusions
It took place in an open-plan area where others could overhear
It was announced the evening before with only "we need to talk"

rubric: Public setting, unverified claims and an anxiety-provoking vague invitation all raise defensiveness.
Using specifics and asking for the employee's view reduce escalation.

items.prompt: A manager has given Lena the same feedback about late weekly reports three times, and the reports are still late. When asked, Lena explains that the data feed she needs is only released on Thursday afternoons, and reports are due Thursday at 5pm. Which diagnosis is best?

options.label: The earlier feedback was too gentle, so a firmer tone would have fixed the lateness
The cause is a process constraint rather than effort, so repeating effort-focused feedback misses it
Lena is resisting the feedback, so the manager should make the consequences more serious
Lena does not understand why deadlines matter, so the manager should explain the business impact

rubric: The lateness stems from a dependency, so feedback should address the process and not motivation.
Other options assume resistance, softness or ignorance that the details do not support.

items.prompt: A manager tells an analyst, "You need to be more proactive." The analyst looks confused, then defensive, and nothing changes. Which analysis best explains the outcome?

options.label: The manager should have first listed the analyst's strengths so the analyst felt safe enough to listen
The feedback was too gentle, so the analyst did not register it as a real performance concern
The feedback named no observable behaviour, so the analyst could not tell what to do differently
The analyst has a fixed mindset, so any developmental comment would have triggered defensiveness

rubric: Vague trait language gives the receiver nothing concrete to act on, which produces confusion and defensiveness.
Distractors blame the person's mindset or the tone rather than the lack of specifics.

items.prompt: A team lead notices that her experienced staff stiffen whenever she opens feedback with praise. Which explanation best fits how the praise-criticism-praise pattern breaks down here?

options.label: Staff prefer to hear the criticism first, because research shows early negatives are always remembered best
Staff feel the praise is too specific, which makes the later criticism seem less credible and less fair
Staff resent any structure in feedback, so any repeated format will produce the same stiffening response
Staff learn to treat the opening praise as a warning, so it is discounted and the real message gets buried

rubric: Once the pattern is recognised, the praise is read as a preamble to criticism and loses value.
Distractors invent absolute claims about specificity or universal preferences.

items.prompt: A developer nodded through a peer's feedback on code reviews but three weeks later nothing has changed. The peer was sincere and the issue was clearly described. Which gap most likely explains this?

options.label: The developer is unwilling to accept criticism from peers and will ignore anything that comes from them
The peer gave too much detail, which overwhelmed the developer and led to nodding without processing
The feedback should have come from a manager, since peers lack the authority needed to change behaviour
The conversation ended without an agreed concrete next step or a checkpoint, so understanding never became action

rubric: Clear description alone does not create change; an agreed action and follow-up are what convert understanding into behaviour.
Distractors assume unwillingness or authority problems without evidence.

items.prompt: A manager corrects a junior colleague's mistake during a team meeting. The colleague goes silent and avoids the manager for days, though the correction was factually accurate. What most plausibly drove the reaction?

options.label: Juniors tend to react badly to any correction from a manager, so the public setting made no real difference
The audience added a status threat that outweighed the content, so the colleague shifted to self-protection
The manager's blunt tone signalled hidden criticism of the colleague's honesty, so the colleague distrusted the feedback itself
The colleague lacked the technical background to follow the correction, so confusion led to the withdrawal afterwards

rubric: An audience turns accurate content into a status threat, shifting attention from learning to self-protection.
Distractors ignore the setting or attribute the reaction to dishonesty or ability.

items.prompt: A manager gave two engineers the same feedback about missed handovers. One engineer was told "the night shift lost two hours reworking the batch" and improved. The other was told "you're careless" and did not. Which factor best explains the difference?

options.label: The second message was shorter, and shorter feedback is always less effective than longer feedback
The first message tied an observable behaviour to its concrete impact, while the second labelled the person
The first engineer is simply more motivated, so the wording of the feedback had little influence
The second message was more critical, and any critical wording reduces performance regardless of content

rubric: Linking behaviour to impact gives meaning and direction, whereas character labels invite defence.
Distractors attribute the difference to motivation or length rather than message structure.

items.prompt: A manager tells a colleague: "Your reports are sloppy and you never seem to care about quality." Which features make this feedback hard to act on? Select all that apply.

options.label: It is delivered privately, which lowers its credibility with the receiver
It points to no specific report or example that anchors the claim
It infers motive ("don't care") instead of describing what was actually observed
It uses "never", an absolute the receiver can rebut with a single counterexample

rubric: Absolutes, inferred motives and missing examples all make the feedback arguable and non-actionable.
Privacy is generally an advantage, not a flaw.

items.prompt: At an annual review, a manager tells a designer that her client handovers have been rushed all year. The designer says, "Nobody ever told me," and becomes withdrawn. The manager's notes show no earlier conversation about it. What is the underlying problem?

options.label: The feedback loop was too infrequent, so the issue surfaced as a surprise rather than a correctable pattern
The designer's handovers are too subjective to assess, so annual reviews should not mention them at all
The manager used too many examples, which made the review feel like a prosecution of the designer
The designer is avoiding responsibility, so the manager should repeat the evidence until she accepts it

rubric: Saving feedback for the annual review removes the chance to correct early and makes it feel like an ambush.
Distractors blame the receiver or the evidence rather than the timing.

items.prompt: A new hire misquoted a price on a client call. A bigger client call is tomorrow. Criteria: timely, private, specific, and builds confidence. Which approach best meets them?

options.label: Say nothing and listen in on tomorrow's call, then correct any errors afterwards if they happen again
Wait for the monthly one-to-one, so the feedback can be combined with other topics in a single session
Send a team email reminding everyone of pricing accuracy, so no individual feels singled out
Meet privately today, describe the specific misquote, and agree how to check prices before tomorrow's call

rubric: A same-day private conversation with a specific example and a plan meets every stated criterion.
Waiting or generic emails fail on timeliness or specificity.

items.prompt: A senior director tells you in passing, "Your presentations lack impact." Criteria: gain usable information, keep the relationship intact, avoid overreacting. Which response is best?

options.label: Accept the comment silently and revise your slides, since asking questions might seem defensive
Explain the constraints you were under, so she understands why the presentations looked as they did
Raise the comment with HR as unclear criticism, so a formal standard can be applied to it
Thank her, then ask for one example and what she would have wanted to see done differently

rubric: Asking for an example and desired change turns vague feedback into usable information without defensiveness.
Explaining constraints reads as defensive; silence yields no information; HR is an overreaction.

items.prompt: Criteria for feedback: describes observable behaviour, states impact, and points to the future. Which draft best meets all three?

options.label: "I felt uncomfortable in the meeting, and I think you probably need to work on your general communication style."
"You were unprofessional in the client meeting on Tuesday, and I expect a much better standard from you next time."
"Clients seem to find you hard to talk to, so try to be more of a listener when you are with them next time."
"In Tuesday's meeting you interrupted the client twice; she lost her thread, so next time let her finish first."

rubric: Only the second names observed behaviour, its effect and a concrete future action.
Others use labels, feelings or hearsay without specific behaviour.

items.prompt: A manager must tell an employee that a recent email to a client came across as dismissive. The tone is ambiguous in writing and the employee is already anxious. Criteria: avoid misreading, keep trust, leave a record. Which plan is best?

options.label: Ask a colleague to hint at the problem first, so the employee has time to prepare a reaction
Send a detailed written critique, so the wording stays precise and can be reread whenever needed
Hold a live conversation to discuss the email, then send a short written summary of what was agreed
Mention it casually in the corridor, so the employee does not feel the matter is formal or serious

rubric: A live conversation reduces tonal misreading and a short follow-up supplies the record.
Pure writing risks misreading; casual or indirect routes lack clarity and respect.

items.prompt: A manager says: "I save all feedback for the quarterly review so it stays formal and fair." Which critique of this approach is strongest against criteria of timeliness and ability to change behaviour?

options.label: Formal reviews are unfair to employees, because written records give them little chance to challenge or add context to what was recorded
Behaviour is hardest to recall and correct weeks later, so errors repeat in the meantime and feedback feels like an ambush
Quarterly reviews make employees anxious about their ratings, so feedback is better replaced by frequent informal praise and no formal review
The approach is sound in most respects, since feedback given too often tends to overwhelm employees and reduce their confidence over time

rubric: Delay weakens specificity and lets problems repeat; surprises erode trust.
Distractors overgeneralise about formality, anxiety or frequency.

items.prompt: After a feedback conversation, which are sound criteria for judging that it went well? Select all that apply.

options.label: The employee still raises problems with the manager openly in later weeks
The employee did not push back at any point during the conversation
The manager covered every item on a prepared list without interruption
The employee can restate the specific behaviour and the agreed next step
The behaviour is checked at a later date and has moved in the agreed direction

rubric: Shared understanding, preserved trust and observed change measure effectiveness.
Silence and completeness of the list are delivery measures, not outcomes.

items.prompt: In a team meeting, a colleague tells you that your status updates are "always late and useless." The content is partly accurate, but the delivery stings and others are watching. Criteria: gain the useful content, keep trust, avoid a public conflict. Which response is best?

options.label: Say nothing now and avoid the colleague afterwards, so the tension has a chance to fade naturally
Acknowledge the lateness briefly, then ask to talk privately about what would make the updates useful
Defend yourself by listing every update you delivered on time, so the room sees the claim is overstated
Tell the colleague that the tone was unacceptable, so everyone hears that such remarks will not be tolerated

rubric: Acknowledging the valid part and moving details to a private talk extracts value and avoids escalation.
Public rebuttal, public rebuke or avoidance each damage trust or lose the information.

items.prompt: A director defends the feedback sandwich (praise, concern, praise) for a senior engineer who keeps skipping design reviews. Criteria: the core message must land, and later praise must stay credible. Which critique is soundest?

options.label: It can bury the concern and teach the engineer to treat praise as a warning sign, so state the issue plainly
It is sound if the opening praise is generic, because specific praise would distract from the concern raised
It fails mainly for senior staff, because experienced people dislike praise and prefer the concern in writing only
It works well, because the praise lowers defensiveness and the concern is still stated once in the middle

rubric: Wrapping a concern in praise dilutes it and makes later praise look like a cushion for bad news.
Distractors assume praise reduces defensiveness or that seniority changes the problem.

items.prompt: After a client pitch went badly, a junior analyst is visibly upset. A second pitch is in two days. Criteria: the feedback must be absorbed and usable before that pitch. Which timing is best?

options.label: Wait until after the second pitch, so the analyst is not distracted and one session can cover both performances together
Acknowledge the difficulty briefly now, then hold the detailed session next morning, leaving time to rehearse changes
Give the full critique in the debrief now, because delay lets the details fade and the analyst may repeat the mistakes in the second pitch
Send detailed written notes tonight, because writing removes emotion and the analyst can read them whenever ready

rubric: Feedback to someone in distress is rarely absorbed; a short delay still leaves time to act before the next pitch.
Distractors over-value immediacy, over-delay, or assume writing alone replaces the conversation.

items.prompt: A lead will receive raw anonymous 360 comments from six reviewers on a five-person team. Criteria: protect trust and keep the feedback actionable. What is the biggest risk of releasing the comments unedited?

options.label: Distinctive wording lets the lead guess authors, so suspicion and defensiveness rise while the real patterns stay unclear
Comments will be too long for the lead to read, so the main themes get lost in the sheer volume of detail
The lead will read the comments as too positive, since anonymity usually encourages polite and vague wording from reviewers
Reviewers will inflate their ratings because they know the comments go straight to the lead without any moderation step

rubric: Small groups and raw verbatim comments make authors guessable, which erodes trust and hides themes.
Distractors name plausible but weaker or unsupported risks.

items.prompt: A peer snaps in front of others: 'Your reports are always a mess.' You suspect one real issue: inconsistent formatting confuses finance. Criteria: protect the working relationship and still learn what is valid. Which response is best?

options.label: Stay calm, ask for one example, take the formatting point on board, and raise the tone privately afterwards
Ignore the remark and quietly fix the formatting, avoiding conflict while still dealing with the likely problem
Agree the reports are a mess and promise a full rewrite, which ends the tension quickly and shows you are open
Say the tone is unacceptable and refuse to discuss the reports until the peer apologises, to set a firm and visible boundary

rubric: Separating content from delivery lets you learn the valid point and address tone later without escalation.
Distractors either reject valid content because of delivery or accept a vague claim wholesale.

items.prompt: Your team includes people for whom criticism in front of others is a serious loss of face. Criteria: the message must stay clear and the relationship intact. Where does 'always be direct' advice break down, and what adjustment is best?

options.label: Directness works everywhere, so keep the same wording but add a longer warm-up to show you value the person
Route the message through the person's manager so nobody loses face and your own relationship stays untouched
Hint at the issue through stories about other people, since the receiver will infer it without being confronted
Keep the content specific but change setting and framing: private, behaviour-focused, standard stated clearly

rubric: Adapting setting and framing preserves a clear message while respecting face norms.
Distractors either ignore the norm, make the message too vague, or avoid owning it.

items.prompt: You are judging whether a draft piece of feedback is ready to deliver. Which are sound grounds for judging it ready? Select all that apply.

options.label: It covers every concern gathered this quarter so nothing needs raising later
It states an effect on the work or team that the receiver may not have seen
It names observable behaviour rather than a judgement about character
It compares the person with a stronger colleague to set a clear benchmark
It concerns something the receiver can realistically change in the coming weeks

rubric: Ready feedback is behavioural, shows impact and is actionable.
Comparisons and bundling every concern undermine focus and trust.

items.prompt: A top salesperson beats quota by 40% but interrupts and belittles colleagues in meetings; two peers have asked to leave the team. You must choose an approach. Criteria: keep the team's trust, be fair to the salesperson, make the expectation unmistakable. Which approach is best?

options.label: Give specific examples and their effect on peers, state it is a performance standard, and agree a check-in date
Ask the peers to give the feedback directly, since the colleagues affected are the ones best placed to be heard
Praise the results and mention the meetings gently, since a star's motivation is fragile and a harsh message might prompt an exit
Wait for the formal review cycle so the concern comes with full performance data and does not look like singling out

rubric: Specific behaviour, impact and a clear standard with follow-up is fair and unmistakable.
Distractors soften the message, delay it, or shift the manager's responsibility onto peers.

items.prompt: Design a 15-minute remote conversation for an employee who goes silent when criticised. Constraints: they must feel in control, hear one specific concern, and leave with one agreed action. Which plan meets all three?

options.label: Send the concern in writing beforehand and stay silent on the call until they respond, so they control the pace fully and nothing is said live
Open with three strengths, list the four main concerns with examples, and email a written action plan after the call
State the purpose and ask permission, give one example with its impact, invite their view, then co-write one dated action
Start with small talk to rebuild rapport, put the concern as a question, and leave any actions for a later session

rubric: Permission, one example, their input and a co-written action satisfy control, specificity and commitment.
Distractors break one constraint: too many concerns, no action, or no real conversation.

items.prompt: Design a team practice that meets three constraints: upward feedback becomes normal, it takes little extra time, and it does not expose junior people. Which design fits?

options.label: Hold an open 'feedback Friday' where everyone gives one spoken critique to a colleague in the room
Set up a suggestion box that HR reviews once a year and summarises for senior leaders only
Managers ask for feedback on one named behaviour in each 1:1, then tell the team what they changed
Run a quarterly anonymous 30-question survey and present the full results at an all-hands meeting

rubric: Asking about one behaviour in existing 1:1s is cheap and models the habit; sharing changes shows it matters.
Other options are costly, expose juniors, or are too rare to make feedback normal.

items.prompt: A manager plans to say: 'You were late to stand-up three times this week. That's unprofessional. Be on time.' The goal is to change behaviour and keep trust. Which addition best fixes what the script lacks?

options.label: A comparison with how punctual the rest of the team has been, so the employee sees the standard clearly
A clear threat of formal consequences, so the employee understands how serious the lateness has become
The effect on the team and a question inviting the employee's explanation, replacing the 'unprofessional' label
A cushioning compliment at the start about the employee's strong output, so the criticism feels less personal

rubric: The script lacks impact and the receiver's perspective, and it uses a label instead of describing behaviour.
Distractors add cushioning, threats or comparison, none of which supply what is missing.

items.prompt: Employees at a firm are regularly shocked by year-end ratings. Constraints: no new formal process, ratings stay annual, and managers must stay honest. Which change best removes the surprises?

options.label: Ask employees to rate themselves before the final rating is set, so they can compare their view with the manager's
Have managers raise any rating-relevant issue in the next 1:1 after noticing it, not hold it for year-end
Share ratings by email a week before the review meeting so people have time to absorb them first
Train managers to soften low ratings with positive language so employees feel less shocked when they hear them

rubric: Raising issues as they occur removes surprise at its source without a new process.
Distractors change timing or wording at the end, or dilute honesty, instead of fixing the missing ongoing feedback.

items.prompt: A team member must tell a director that overruling decisions in public is hurting delivery. Constraints: low retaliation risk, specific, and usable by the director. Which plan fits?

options.label: Tell the director's manager first so the message arrives with authority and the director is less likely to retaliate
Ask for a private moment, cite one recent decision and its effect on delivery, then propose another way to escalate
Send an anonymous note listing each occasion in the past year, so the director sees the scale of the pattern safely
Raise it in the next all-hands Q&A, so the director hears that others share the concern and finds it harder to dismiss

rubric: A private, specific example with impact and an alternative is usable and lowers risk.
Distractors are public, anonymous and unspecific, or bypass the director.

items.prompt: A manager is designing a conversation to correct a pattern of missed deadlines while preserving trust. Which elements should the plan include? Select all that apply.

options.label: A full history of the employee's past missed deadlines, presented first to establish that the pattern is real and not a one-off
A closing agreement on a concrete next step, owned by the employee, with a date to review progress together
A specific recent example and its effect on the team, stated factually before any interpretation of the cause
A settled conclusion about the cause of the delays, prepared in advance so the conversation stays short and focused
An opening that states the purpose, then invites the employee's view of what is getting in the way before solutions are set

rubric: Purpose and permission, a specific example with impact, and a dated next step build clarity and trust.
A fixed verdict and a list of past mistakes shut down dialogue and feel like an attack.

items.prompt: A manager gets two credible pieces of feedback about Priya: one reviewer says she 'dominates' meetings, another says she is 'too quiet.' Constraints: don't dismiss either, don't confuse Priya, and produce something testable. Which plan meets them?

options.label: Ask each reviewer for concrete examples, look for contexts that explain the split, and agree a small experiment with Priya
Discard both comments because they contradict, and collect fresh feedback next year from a larger and more varied group
Tell Priya both comments, ask her to pick the one she agrees with, and work on only that one this year
Average the two comments, tell Priya she is about right, and move on to other development topics for the year

rubric: Examples reveal context-specific patterns, and a small experiment makes the response testable and clear to Priya.
Distractors dismiss the data, average it meaninglessly, or hand Priya an unresolved choice.
